abstract.t: This document discusses the drawbacks of the current practice of assigning a UDP port to each multicast application. Such assignments are redundant because the multicast group address already uniquely identifies the data. The document assigns a UDP port specifically for use with multicast applications and lists requirements for using this port. This approach provides immediate compatibility with existing protocol stacks, while also requiring improvements to make the port easier to use.

section.title: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

This document uses the term "multicast group address" to refer collectively to the IP destination address for Any-Source Multicast (ASM) , and the { source, destination } pair for Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) , since they serve the same functional purpose. Both exist to identify a stream of packets related to a particular activity. The network's multicast routing infrastructure uses the multicast group address to identify where packets should be forwarded, to deliver them efficiently to all members of the group that need to receive these packets, while avoiding delivering the packets to hosts or networks that do not need to receive them.

This document describes each separate usage of an application as an "instantiation" of that application. For example, a multicast videoconferencing application may be in use all over the world for a thousand different videoconference meetings at the same time. It would be terribly inefficient (and would defeat the purpose of multicast) if all the meetings were to use the same multicast group, and all copies of the application were to receive all the traffic for all videoconference meetings taking place at that time. Consequently, each instantiation of a multicast application requires its own unique multicast group address. How a unique multicast group addresses is assigned for each instantiation is the scope of other existing IETF documents, such as the guidelines for IPv4 multicast address assignment
and for IPv6 multicast address assignment .

section.title: Introduction
section.t:
The Internet community has recognized the need to be judicious when assigning port numbers (). With unicast applications, the need for explicit port assignment has been reduced by techniques such as locally assigning a dynamic port, combined with some mechanism for advertising that port
(). Dynamic assignment does not work with multicast applications because it is impossible to guarantee that the port remains unused by all hosts that may want to join a given multicast group. The result is that traditionally each multicast application-layer protocol has had to have its own dedicated port assignment. Even worse, each instantiation of that multicast application-layer protocol needs to have a different unique port assigned.

Astute readers may observe that the previous statement is not strictly true. In the TCP/IP model, the port number in the transport layer multiplexes unicast traffic destined to different applications within a host (, ). With multicast, the use of a port number to multiplex applications is unnecessary because the multicast group address already provides a unique identifier for each application instantiation within a given multicast scope. Techniques like SO_REUSEPORT (details vary depending on the specific network API) already exist and are already used to allow multiple copies of the same multicast application to run on the same host and share a single UDP port. This observation is the inspiration behind this specification. If multiple instantiations of the same application can share a single port, then, by the same logic, all multicast applications can share a single port as long as they cooperate and use the appropriate API mechanisms to share the port. This specification codifies this existing practice of sharing a port, and assigns a single UDP port that may be used by all multicast applications: the Multicast Application Port.

Multicast applications can follow the guidance in this specification immediately to use the Multicast Application Port on any platform that supports SO_REUSEPORT or equivalent (). For example, this technique is widely used to run multiple independent implementations of Multicast DNS on a single device. In addition, network protocol stacks and APIs can assist in the future development of such applications by enforcing special rules to ensure correct use of the Multicast Application Port. This helps detect and prevent inadvertent application bugs that would interfere with the correct sharing of this port (). Deployment of these special protections is expected to take place incrementally, but applications are free to use the Multicast Application Port without waiting for host APIs to begin enforcing the protections.
The Multicast Application Port can be used with both IPv6 and IPv4.

In effect, the Multicast Application Port becomes a vestigial placeholder value, present only because the UDP packet format requires a value in the destination port field. At best, it signifies merely that this traffic is multicast. However, even that information is redundant, since the fact that the traffic is multicast can be inferred by observing that the destination IP address is a multicast address.

Use of this port is optional because there may be circumstances where assigning a port is preferred, such as when participants cannot meet the requirements in and , or when a firewall blocks a traffic pattern used by the application ().

An application sending multicast messages using the Multicast Application Port as the destination port MAY also send unicast messages using a different destination port. One possible benefit of doing so is to balance out deficiencies related to multicast distribution .

section.title: Multicast Address Assignment
section.t:
The ability to identify a multicast application instantiation by its multicast group address assumes that a unique multicast group address has been assigned to the application instantiation. These assignments are outside the scope of this document. Additional information can be obtained from the overview of the Internet multicast addressing architecture
and the following IANA registry groups:

section.title: Assignment
section.t: This document requests assignment of UDP port 8738 (0x2222) and gives it the service name "multicast-app".

ASM applications using the Multicast Application Port are identified by the destination multicast address. SSM applications using the Multicast Application Port are identified by their (S,G) channel, a combination of source unicast address and destination multicast address . As such, the Multicast Application Port MUST NOT be used as either a source port or destination port for any non-multicast messages.
The Multicast Application Port MAY be used as a source port by an application that exclusively uses multicast messages.

If any application messages are unicast, then it is RECOMMENDED that the source port used for multicast messages be set to the port that receivers can send unicast replies to. Note that such arrangements would likely require receivers to use multiple sockets, as the application would need to bind to multiple ports.

section.title: Application Requirements
section.t: Applications can use the Multicast Application Port by meeting the requirements in this section.

Applications SHALL NOT prevent other applications from using this port. On hosts using POSIX-like socket APIs , this is typically accomplished by enabling a socket option before binding the socket. Common socket options include SO_REUSEADDR, SO_REUSEPORT, and SO_REUSE_MULTICASTPORT, but each platform provides its own method.
Applications SHALL NOT send any non-multicast messages using the Multicast Application Port as either a source port or destination port.

Applications SHALL discard all non-multicast datagrams received on the Multicast Application Port. Furthermore, applications SHALL discard all datagrams received on the Multicast Application Port that are not addressed to the multicast group address and interface being used by that application instantiation. Related socket APIs are described in “Socket Interface Extensions for Multicast Source Filters” .

section.title: Host Requirements
section.t: Hosts implementing this specification SHALL require applications using this port to use it non-exclusively. On hosts using POSIX-like socket APIs , this is typically accomplished by enabling a socket option before binding the socket. Common socket options include SO_REUSEADDR, SO_REUSEPORT, and SO_REUSE_MULTICASTPORT, but each platform provides its own method. This requirement ensures that applications developed on a conformant host will follow the correct rules, and also ensures that such applications will also work correctly on older hosts that do not enforce the protections on the Multicast Application Port.

If the application fails to follow the correct steps to share the Multicast Application Port, then the networking API SHALL return an error code, throw an exception, or otherwise fail the application’s attempt to bind to the Multicast Application Port. This helps the application programmer discover their mistake and correct it. If the application fails to follow the correct steps then the networking API MUST NOT try to be “helpful” by silently correcting the misbehaving application and automatically granting it shared access to the Multicast Application Port. This would be counter to the intention of ensuring that a properly written application will work both on a platform that implements protection for the Multicast Application Port, and on older systems that have not been updated to implement these Multicast Application Port host requirements.
Hosts SHALL prevent use of the port with the wildcard address () by having the socket bind operation return an error code.
Hosts SHALL prevent applications from sending non-multicast packets using the Multicast Application Port as either a source or destination port by having the send operation return an error code.
Hosts SHALL discard all incoming, non-multicast packets that use the Multicast Application Port as either a source or destination port.

Hosts SHOULD deliver to an application endpoint (e.g., socket) only packets addressed to the multicast group address to which the application endpoint has subscribed. (Technically this is not essential, since applications are required to discard all datagrams received on the Multicast Application Port that are not addressed to the multicast group address to which it subscribed. However, it is advisable for efficiency, since it is wasteful to deliver packets to an application only to have that application promptly discard them.)

section.title: Firewall Considerations
section.t: Many network firewalls, which operate on network infrastructure, and host firewalls, which operate on individual hosts, are configured to accept incoming messages as long as there was first an outgoing message using the same set of ports . Consider the following sequence of messages:

ol.li:
(Multicast) Host A to group containing Host B
Source Port: 50000 (Dynamic)
Dest Port: 8738

(Unicast) Host B to Host A
Source Port: 60000 (Dynamic)
Dest Port: 50000

(Unicast) Host A to Host B
Source Port: 50000
Dest Port: 60000

section.t: A host firewall running on Host A (or a network firewall between Host A and Host B) may block Message 2 because it uses a different set of ports than Message 1 uses.

While a firewall could be configured to accept Message 2, this configuration would have to be automated because the use of dynamic ports makes manual configuration too costly even in small deployments. However, this automation leads to unacceptable security risks. For example, if a firewall were to respond to Message 1 by opening up the source port used in the message, a malicious application running on the host could open large holes in the firewall by repeatedly sending variations of Message 1 using different source ports.
Host firewalls could be configured to allow messages associated with a given application (instead of specific ports), but this approach would not work with a network firewall.

Ultimately, the current practice of assigning a multicast application its own port is more practical for any application that uses both multicast and unicast messages and could be deployed in an environment using firewalls. Firewall configuration with an assigned port is straightforward: allow all messages using that port.

section.title: Implementation Status
section.t: Note to RFC Editor: please remove this entire section before publication, as well as the reference to RFC7942.

This section records the status of known implementations of the protocol defined by this specification at the time of posting of this Internet-Draft, and is based on the IETF's guidance on improving awareness of running code . The description of implementations in this section is intended to assist the IETF in its decision processes in progressing drafts to RFCs. Please note that the listing of any individual implementation here does not imply endorsement by the IETF. Furthermore, no effort has been spent to verify the information presented here that was supplied by IETF contributors. This is not intended as, and must not be construed to be, a catalog of available implementations or their features. Readers are advised to note that other implementations may exist.

According to that guidance, "this will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature. It is up to the individual working groups to use this information as they see fit".

Prototypes for Linux, macOS, and Windows are available at . These programs configure a socket to receive messages sent to the Multicast Application Port using a specified multicast address. Another program, such as socat, can be used to send messages and demonstrate, with an unmodified operating system, that the prototype will 1) display messages sent to the Multicast Application Port using the specified multicast address, and 2) not display messages sent to the Multicast Application Port, but using a different multicast address.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: Firewall rules referencing ports are typically intended to match specific applications for filtering and QoS. Because applications using the Multicast Application Port are identified by their destination multicast address (ASM) or (S,G) channel (SSM), then rules referencing the Multicast Application Port SHOULD also consider the applicable network layer address(es). A firewall rule that only references the Multicast Application Port would match all applications using that port, which is too broadly-scoped.

Applications running on a host that does not protect the Multicast Application Port from misuse are vulnerable to a denial of service attack if another application claims exclusive access to the port. This vulnerability is not unique to the Multicast Application Port. Regardless of what port is used by a multicast application, a malicious application could claim exclusive access to that port first, and thereby prevent the legitimate application from being able to use its port.

Systems that use POSIX-like socket APIs typically have restrictions on binding multiple sockets to the same port. This can serve as a rudimentary security mechanism in that other local applications cannot eavesdrop on the multicast stream. A necessary side-effect of using the Multicast Application Port is that applications can no longer rely on these security mechanisms. These applications may want to incorporate additional security measures into their protocol. Note that the problem of local eavesdropping is typically no worse than eavesdropping in-flight, so it is likely that both attack vectors can be resolved by the same security measure.

section.title: IANA Considerations
section.t: IANA is requested to assign the following port:
section.artwork: Service Name multicast-app Transport Protocol UDP Assignee IESG <iesg@ietf.org> Contact IETF Chair <chair@ietf.org> Description Multicast Application Port Reference This document Port Number 8738
section.t: IANA is requested to update its "Application for Service Names and User Port Numbers" to reference this document and ask the applicant if the Multicast Application Port may be used. These changes will help applicants understand that it may not be necessary or beneficial to assign a port for their multicast protocol.
